list.listitem: In patients older than 50 years, systolic blood pressure (SBP) more than 140 mm Hg is a much more important risk factor for cardiovascular disease than diastolic blood pressure (DBP). AB
Patients with suspected hypertension should have the diagnosis confirmed using ambulatory BP monitoring. B

Most patients with hypertension have essential hypertension, and more extensive testing for secondary hypertension is not necessary unless BP control is not achieved or if the patient has symptoms of catecholamine excess, bruits, or unprovoked hypokalemia. B
Lifestyle modification (smoking cessation, sodium restriction, exercise, weight control, etc.) lowers BP and should be encouraged in all patients with all stages of hypertension. A

Initial therapy options include a thiazide diuretic, calcium channel blocker (CCB), angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, or angiotensin receptor blocker for non-black patients, and a thiazide or CCB for black patients according to ACC guidelines. A
Patients with chronic kidney disease should receive an ACE or ARB, while those with heart failure should receive a thiazide and ACE inhibitor preferentially over a CCB. A
Aldosterone or amiloride are good options for patients with resistant hypertension. B

background.definition: The diagnosis of essential hypertension is based on the average of two or more properly measured, seated BP readings on each of two or more office visits. Hypertensive crises or emergencies exist when patients experience marked BP elevations and acute target organ damage. Isolated systolic hypertension is defined when the systolic pressure is above 140 mm Hg and the diastolic pressure is less than 90 mm Hg.

list.listitem: Among normotensive adults, after 10 years 20% developed hypertension, with higher incidence in patients who smoked and with higher body mass index.
Approximately 72 million adults in the United States are hypertensive; 1 out of 3 adults.
Ninety five percent of people with hypertension have essential hypertension.
In the Framingham Heart Study, among patients without hypertension between the ages of 55 and 65 years who survive into their 80s, 80% to 90% will develop hypertension.
Estimated total costs in 2007 were $66.4 billion.
Worldwide, 7.6 million premature deaths, about 54% of strokes and 47% of ischemic heart disease are attributable to high BP.
Hypertension is present in 69% of patients presenting with their first myocardial infarction, 77% of patients with an initial stroke, and 74% of patients who develop heart failure.
Most patients with hypertension have essential hypertension (cause is unknown).
Tobacco use, salt intake, obesity, and alcohol intake increase risk.
In the Framingham study, a 5% increase in weight was associated with a 20% to 30% increase in the odds of progression to hypertension.
Salt sensitivity: about 60% of people with hypertension respond to a reduction in salt intake. This is implicated in some secondary causes of hypertension.
Genetic predisposition.
Work stress and caffeine intake do not appear to have any meaningful effect on BP.
BP may be transiently increased in patients who are in pain, who are anxious, and who are taking medications such as decongestants, cyclosporine, and NSAIDs.
Multifactorial.
Key interplay between renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, autonomic nervous system, bradykinin, endothelin, nitric oxide, atrial natriuretic peptide, ouabain.
Genetic predisposition is an area of active investigation.
Initial increase in cardiac output, subsequent increase in systemic vascular resistance resulting in a chronic elevation of BP.
Dietary salt intake of a population corresponds to the prevalence of hypertension worldwide.
The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for high BP in adults 18 years and older. The diagnosis should be confirmed using ambulatory monitoring. A
They found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against screening in children although blood pressure measurement is a routine part of medical care of children. B .
A Cochrane review concluded that it is unclear that treating mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy is effective. A
Children older than 3 years who are seen in medical care settings should have their BP measured at least once during every health care episode. C
Encourage patients with prehypertension to reduce stop smoking, reduce sodium intake, adopt Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet, increase exercise, and lose weight. C
Hypertension is defined as the average of two or more proper measurements of BP in the office over 140/90 or over 130-135/80 in patients with heart disease or diabetes. A
USPSTF guidelines recommend ambulatory monitoring to confirm elevated blood pressure in all patients.A
Self-monitoring of BP at home or work is a practical way to assess differences between out of office and office readings. B

list.listitem: Hypertension is defined when the average BP is greater than 140 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg diastolic.
Isolated systolic hypertension is defined when the systolic pressure is above 160 mm Hg and the diastolic pressure is less than 90 mm Hg.

BP is further classified for adults based on the highest reading of the following: normal is less than 120/80; prehypertension is 120-129/80-89; Stage 1 hypertension is 140-159/90-99; and Stage 2 hypertension is greater than 160/100.

Most patients with hypertension have no symptoms and no physical findings other than elevated BP. Retinal findings are specific but not sensitive for hypertension, but are important findings that require referral to an ophthalmologist.
The presence or absence of headaches should not be used as an indicator of BP control.
Patients with essential hypertension should be examined for clues to possible causes of secondary hypertension and for target organ damage (ie, retinal findings, abdominal bruit, ECG).

Isolated diastolic hypertension (systolic BP <140 mm Hg and diastolic BP >90 mm Hg) is present in 6% of patients but is not associated in a large prospective cohort study with cardiovascular disease, heart failure, kidney disease, or mortality.

A systematic review of 23 studies with 4210 children and adolescents identifed risk factors associated with the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with secondary hypertension. The overall prevalence of secondary hypertension in children was 9% in primary care settings and 44% in referral settings. Another systematic review found that 4% of children in primary care settings and 20% in specialty clinics have secondary hypertension.

Demographic findings most associated with secondary hypertension included a family history of secondary hypertension (LR+ 4.7), a history of prematurity (LR+ range 2.3 - 2.8), and age 6 years or younger (LR+ range 2.2 - 2.6). A family history of primary hypertension was associated with a lower likelihood of secondary hypertension (LR- 0.49). Clinical and laboratory findings most associated with secondary hypertension included a body weight at the 10% or lower level for age and sex (LR+ 4.5), microalbuminuria (LR+ 13), and a serum uric acid concentration of 5.5 mg/dL or lower with normal renal function (LR+ range 2.1 - 6.3). Clinical findings associated with a decreased likelihood of secondary hypertension included obesity (LR- 0.34) and the absence of hypertension-related symptoms (eg, headache, blurry vision, dizziness, chest pain, edema; LR- range 0.19 - 0.36).

The auscultatory method of systolic and diastolic BP measurement with a calibrated and validated instrument should be used. Persons should be seated quietly for at least 5 minutes with feet on the floor, and arm supported at heart level. An appropriate-sized cuff (cuff bladder encircling at least 80% of the arm) should be used to ensure accuracy. At least two measurements should be made, as a study found that the first systolic BP is 10 mm Hg or more higher in many patients.

USPSTF guidelines recommend ambulatory monitoring to confirm elevated blood pressure in all patients. While an automated cuff is preferred, serial home measurements by the patient may be adequate. Therapy may be initiated for those with very elevated blood pressure prior to ambulatory monitoring (>185/110).
Measuring blood pressures on a bare arm is best. It is also important to support the arm. An unsupported arm yielded blood pressures that are 4 to 6 mm higher in a study of 133 adult.

A study of 195 patients found that using a regular cuff on larger-than-average arms can falsely raise blood pressure readings by almost 5 mmHg, and a regular cuff on an especially thin arm can lower readings by 3.6 mm Hg. More than half of this study group, which had a mean body mass index lower than the U.S. average, required a large or extra-large cuff.

There is some evidence that automated measurement in the primary care office may be more accurate than manual measurement. One study found randomized 555 patients in 67 offices to automated or manual measurement, and found that manual measurement was more likely to overestimate the SBP (6 mm vs 2 mm) when compared with 24 hour ambulatory monitoring performed in all of the patients.

A systematic review identified 31 studies with 9279 participants comparing automated in office measurement or manual measurement with ambulatory blood pressures as the reference standard. They found that the manual office measurements were 13.4/5.9 mm Hg higher than the ambulatory measurements, but that the ambulatory and automated in office measurements were the same.
Both US and European guidelines state that a clinic blood pressure of 160/90 is equivalent to home or ambulatory blood pressure of 145/90.
A single blood pressure measurement should not be used to diagnose hypertension. There is insufficient evidence to recommend ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in pregnancy.

At the time of diagnosis, patients with hypertension should have several tests to look for target organ damage and common comorbid conditions: 12-lead ECG, UA, blood glucose, hematocrit, serum potassium, calcium, creatinine (or glomerular filtration rate), fasting lipid profile and in patients with known diabetes or renal disease the microalbumin/creatinine ratio.

Most patients with hypertension have essential hypertension, and more extensive testing for secondary hypertension is not necessary unless BP control is not achieved or if the patient has symptoms of catecholamine excess, bruits, or unprovoked hypokalemia. See chapter on secondary hypertension for a more detailed discussion.
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is more informative than clinic readings in predicting mortality outcomes.
A clinical decision rule using factors such as age, gender, presence of bruits, etc, can be used to identify patients at higher risk of having renovascular hypertension.
Since BP may be transiently elevated, the diagnosis of essential hypertension is based on the average of two or more properly measured seated readings on each of two or more office visits.

Ambulatory BP monitoring (24-hour continuous BP monitoring) should be used in suspected white-coat hypertension, patients with hypertension and no target organ damage, apparent drug resistance, hypotensive symptoms with antihypertensive medication, episodic hypertension, and autonomic dysfunction.

Self-monitoring of BP is a practical way to assess differences between out of office and office readings. In patients whose out of office BPs are consistently less than 130/80 and who lack signs of target organ damage, ambulatory monitoring, and drug therapy can be avoided.
Self-measurement or ambulatory monitoring is also helpful in smokers since smoking acutely raises BP for about 15 minutes.
Lifestyle modification (eg, smoking cessation, sodium restriction, exercise, weight control) lowers BP and should be encouraged in all patients with all stages of hypertension. A
ACC/AHA guidelines advocate a target of 130/80 for most hypertensive adults including those with diabetes, CKD, or >10% 10 year CV risk.A

Initial therapy options include a low dose of a thiazide diuretic or calcium channel blocker (CCB), paired with an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker in a single pill.A
Patients with chronic kidney disease should receive an ACE or ARB, while those with heart failure should receive a thiazide and ACE inhibitor preferentially over a CCB.A
Reducing the number of daily doses increases adherence to BP lowering medication. A
Intensive BP lowering (< 130/80) improves cardiovascular outcomes (NNT = 58) while increasing hypotension and syncope (NNH = 55). A
Aldosterone or amiloride are good options for patients with resistant hypertension. B

The ACC/AHA guidelines (2025) recommend using the PREVENT risk score to estimate 10 and 30 year risk for CV events as part of the evaluation. For stage 1 hypertension (130-139/80-89) medical therapy should be initiated for those with a > 7.5% 10-year CV risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease. Initiate therapy with a low dose combination of an ACE or ARB combined with HCTZ or a CCB. Screen for primary aldosteronism in all patients with resistant hypertension, and consider GLP-1 RAs for patients who are obese.

The 2017 guidelines published by the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association advocate for a target blood pressure of 130/80 with drug treatment recommended for patients exceeding those values if they have diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or a >10% 10 year risk of cardiovascular disease. This guideline has not been endorsed by other primary care physician societies, in part out of concern for overtreatment.

A guideline from Hypertension Canada (2025) recommends a treatment target of 140/90 for most patients, and systolic 130 to 139 for patients at high cardiovascular risk. A target of < 130 mm systolic if recommended but only if well tolerated. Initial therapy should begin with low dose combination therapy choosing 2 out of ACEI, ARB, thiazide diurtics, and long-acting dihyopyridine CCBs.
In general, those patients with the highest risk for cardiovascular events benefit the greatest from antihypertensive therapies.

A report comparing European and ACC/AHA guidelines concluded that they were generally similar with the exception that 130-130/80-89 was defined as stage 1 hypertension by US guidelines requiring treatment for higher risk persons, while it was defined as high normal by European guidelines.

The ACC/AHA guidelines that recommend a 130/80 target for most patients are based largely on the SPRINT trial, a large study that demonstrated a net benefit in older, non-diabetic individuals treated to a more aggressive systolic blood pressure target of 120 mm Hg; more episodes of hypotension and syncope were noted in the aggressive treatment group.

Intensive BP control (SBP <140 mm Hg) is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events, stroke, or worsening microvascular disease; no impact on the risk of myocardial infarction, heart failure, or mortality was noted relative to standard care.

In addition, the CARDIO-CIS study randomized non-diabetics to a SBP target of 130 versus 140, and found fewer adverse events in those with the lower target. However, they used a very broad composite outcome that included 13 different types of events, and the study was open-label, which biases in favor of the intervention.
However, a Cochrane review concluded that in the general population with hypertension, the benefits of lower targets do not outweigh the harms.

A meta-analysis of 25 studies with up to 5 year follow-up found that in patients with coronary artery disease, use of antihypertensives in patients with BP less than 140/90 mm Hg improves cardiovascular outcomes (NNT = 77 for cardiovascular mortality and 67 for all cause mortality). It is not clear whether this is because of BP lowering effects or other known beneficial effects of drugs like beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (the study did not find a difference between drug classes, though).
A meta-analysis suggested thata target range for SBP between 140 and 150 mm Hg is ideal for patients with diabetes.

A cohort study of 570 residents 85 years and older taking an antihypertensive found an association between lower systolic blood pressure and increased all cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.29 per 10 mm Hg lower BP).

A Japanese study randomized 1263 adults with a stroke in the past 3 years to intensive control (target 120/80) or usual care (target 140/90). The target blood pressure was achieved in 62% of the standard treatment patients compared with 32% of the intensively treated patients. At the end of the study, the annual rate of first subsequent stroke was 2.3% in the standard treatment group and 1.6% in the intensive treatment group, but this was not statistically significant.

An observational study using VA hospital data found that the intensification of antihypertensive regimens on discharge in older adults hospitalized for noncardiac conditions is associated with an increased risk of readmission (NNTH = 27) and medication-related serious adverse events (NNTH = 63) within 30 days. Moreover, there is no association with a decreased risk of cardiovascular events at 1 year. A second study by the same group (also in the VA) found similar potential harms with intensive blood pressure control in hospitalized patients, but not in patients with an initial BP of 180 mm Hg or higher.

A randomized trial with 7490 patients compared hypotension avoidance with hypertension avoidance strategies following noncardiac surgery in the perioperative period. There was no difference between the 2 groups in clinically important hypotension during the postoperative period, despite the different strategies.

In hospitalized older adults, intensive treatment of hypertension was associated with an increased risk for adverse cardiac events, specifically acute kidney injury, transfer to ICU, and elevation of troponin and BNP levels. This association was not seen in the subgroup of patients with a maximum BP of 180 mmHg or greater during initial hospitalization.

Thiazide diuretics should be used as initial therapy for non-black hypertensive patients, including those with diabetes. Calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are also reasonable alternative in these patients. In black patients, thiazide-type diuretics or calcium channel blockers are reasonable first choices. In adults with chronic kidney disease, ACE-inhibitors or ARBs are appropriate first choices. You should give up to 3 drugs in a recommended class (see ) before considering drugs that are not in a recommended class.

A study randomized 13,523 VA participants to continuing to take HCTZ or switching to chlorthalidone at half the dose. Overall, there was no difference in a composite of nonfatal MI, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, urgent revascularization, or non-cancer death. However, the subset with a history of MI or stroke at baseline had fewer primary outcome events with chlorthalidone (14.3% vs 19.4%; HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 - 0.94; NNT = 20), while those without that history had a slightly higher likelihood of the primary outcome with chlorthalidone (9.9% vs 8.9%; HR 1.12; 95% CI 1.0 - 1.26). The authors note that they believe this difference was mostly likely a chance finding. Chlorthalidone use was associated with a significantly higher risk of hypokalemia (6.0% vs 4.4%; NNTH = 62), including severe hypokalemia of less than 3.1 mmol/L (5.0% vs 3.6%; HR 1.39; 95% CI 1.18 - 1.64; NNTH = 71).

Using an ACE-inhibitor and ARB in combination is not recommended, nor is using beta blockers or alpha blockers as initial treatment. There is no added benefit to mortality reduction in patients treated with a combination of ACE inhibitors and ARBs, but there is a higher risk of adverse events such as hyperkalemia or hypotension.

Hydralazine lowers BP but their effect on clinical outcomes has not been studied in RCTs. Loop diuretics have a modest effect in lowering blood pressure, but are not generally recommended as an agents for patients with essential hypertension.

Recent studies suggest minimal outcome benefit in treating subjects with mild hypertension (defined as 140-159/90-99 mm Hg). However, they largely used older agents such as beta-blockers. A review found that beta blockers used first line in essential hypertension failed to render any mortality benefit and only a modest reduction in cardiovascular disease incidence.

As a class of antihypertensives, calcium channel blockers reduced deaths similar to other medicines, and may reduce total cardiovascular events compared to beta blockers. Calcium channel blockers may reduce stroke more than ACE-inhibitors or ARBs but may increase heart failure events when compared to these agents.
The relative efficacy of beta-blockers as a second-line drug in addition to diuretics has also been questioned; this may be due to less effect on reducing pulse pressure.
Cardioselective beta blockers appear to be safe in patients who also have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Reducing the number of daily doses increases adherence to BP lowering medication. However, automated text reminders do not improve adherence based on a randomized trial with 151 patients with out of range blood pressure control.

In a trial of patient without indications for blood pressure medicine or lipid lowering, giving them an antihypertensive combination and rosuvastatin did not decrease the likelihood of cognitive decline.
Resistant hypertension is generally defined as inadequate BP control with 3 or more medications.

Spironolactone has been shown to be an effective add-on therapy if the blood pressure is not controlled after maximizing doses of three drugs. A guideline from Hypertension Canada (2025) recommends spironolactone as the initial agent for resistant hypertension.

A trial randomized 118 patients with resistant hypertension to amiloride 5 mg or spironolactone 12.5 mg, both once daily, and then adjusted as necessary to target SBP < 130 mm Hg. Both reduced BP similarly (-14 mm Hg).

A trial randomized 796 patients with systolic BP between 140 and 170 mm Hg tothe aldosterone synthase inhibitor baxdrostat 1 mg, 2 mg, or placebo. After 3 months, the mean reduction in systolic BP from baseline was -15 mm for 1 mg baxdrostat, -16 mm for 2 mg, and -6 mm for placebo. Hyperkalemia > 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 2.3% with the 1 mg dose and 3% with the 2 mg dose.

Lorundrostat is another aldosterone synthase inhibitor. In a RCT with 285 participants with resistant hypertension, after 3 months the systolic BP decreased 15 mm in the lorundrostat 50 mg group and -7 mm in the placebo group. Hyperkalemia with K+ > 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 5%.
Renal denervation is another treatment option for resistant hypertension. A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs with 2478 patients found a 4.4 mm average reduction in systolic BP.

A Spanish study randomized 19,168 adults with hypertension to evening vs morning administration of their blood pressure medications. After 6 years, using intention-to-treat analysis significantly fewer patients in the bedtime group experienced the primary cardiovascular disease outcome compared with the awakening group (adjusted HR = 0.55; 95% CI 0.50-0.61; NNT = 20). These findings have been criticized for issues with the trial design and conduct.

However, the subsequent TIME study in the UK randomized over 21,000 persons with hypertension to morning (6 am to 10 am) or evening (8 pm to 12 pm) administration. They found no difference in any CV or mortality outcomes after 5 years follow-up.

Similarly, the BedMed trial randomized 3357 patients to morning or evening administration of BP meds, and after 4.6 years there was no difference in a composite of all-cause death, stroke, acute coronary syndrome, or heart failure between the bedtime and the morning groups (2.3 vs 2.4 events per 100 patient-years, respectively).
Antiplatelet agents

A Cochrane review found no evidence that antiplatelet agents (primarily aspirin) reduce mortality, although they may reduce the likelihood of cardiovascular events. A limitation of this review is that they combined studies of primary and secondary prevention.

Most obese patients undergoing bariatric surgery have improvements in hypertension. In one study of 100 obese patients (BMI 30-39.9) with hypertension who underwent Roux-en-Y bypass, 35% were normotensive 3 years later.

In patients with refractory hypertension because of renal artery stenosis but a physician assessment that surgery would be of uncertain benefit, an RCT found no benefit of surgery over medical therapy. A recent study found no added benefit over medical therapy to stent stenotic renal arteries in subjects with hypertension or chronic kidney disease.
An RCT found that endovascular renal denervation modestly lowers blood pressure more than a sham procedure (6/2 mm Hg) but there has been no long-term follow-up.
Aerobic exercise of any type produces small but significant reduction in BP regardless of body mass, ethnic group, or age.
There is insufficient evidence to support whether garlic impacts blood pressure.
Vitamin D supplementation does not appear to impact isolated systolic hypertension in older adults with low vitamin D levels.
Coenzyme Q10 does not have a clinically significant impact on blood pressure.
A Cochrane review found very little evidence regarding efficacy of the herbal Roselle for lowering blood pressure.
Patients who smoke should be encouraged to quit.
Telephone follow up for patients with diabetes does not increase adherence to antihypertensive therapy.
In obese patients with hypertension, losing 10 kg results in lowering BP an average of 6 mm Hg systolic and 5 mm Hg diastolic.
However, a Cochrane review concluded that it is not known whether this weight reduction is associated with less morbidity or mortality.
Modest reduction in salt intake for 4 or more weeks significantly lowers BP in patients with elevated BP.

Salt restriction has not been shown to decrease mortality or cardiovascular morbidity in patients with cardiovascular disease. From a population viewpoint, salt reduction may have some benefit in reducing the overall cardiovascular disease burden.
The DASH diet, which is rich in fruits and vegetables and low in fat lowers BP 5 to 10 mm Hg.
Lifestyle modification improves short-term BP control.
Interventions such as self-monitoring and appointment reminders within an organized system of care can improve BP control in hypertensive patients.
Patients co-managed with a pharmacist are more likely to achieve BP goals than those managed by usual care (55% vs 20%, P <0.001, NNT = 3).
Treating obstructive sleep apnea with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy is associated with improved blood pressure control.

A retrospective cohort study identified older patients with elevanted BP during the first 48 hours of hospitalization. They found that intensive treatment of elevated BP in asymptomatic hospitalized older adults was associated with an increased risk of adverse events, specifically acute kidney injury, transfer to intensive care, and elevation of troponin and BNP levels. This association was not seen in the subgroup of patients with a maximum BP of 180 mmHg or greater during initial hospitalization.

A randomized trial compared hypotension avoidance with hypertension avoidance strategies in 7490 hospitalized patients. They found no difference in outcomes when comparing 2 different blood pressure management strategies — hypotension avoidance and hypertension avoidance — in the perioperative period. Adherence to the strategies, however, was suboptimal. Additionally, there was no difference between the 2 groups in clinically important hypotension during the postoperative period, despite the different strategies.
In patients older than 50 years, SBP greater than 140 mm Hg is a much more important risk factor for cardiovascular disease than DBP. A

BP should be treated to a target BP less than 140/90 to decrease cardiovascular complications. Patients with hypertension and coexisting diabetes or kidney disease should have their BP lowered to less than 130/80. A

In patients with stage 1 hypertension and additional cardiac risk factors, achieving a sustained reduction of 12 mm Hg in SBP over 10 years will prevent 1 death for every 11 patients treated. In patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease or target organ damage treating nine patients for 10 years will prevent 1 death. A
The risk of cardiovascular disease beginning at 115/75 mm Hg doubles with each increment of 20/10.
In men with untreated or inadequately treated BP whose SBP is over 140, cardiovascular disease mortality is double that for men with controlled hypertension.
Pulse pressure and SBP are better predictors of developing congestive heart failure than DBP.

In patients older than 50 years, SBP greater than 140 mm Hg is a much more important risk factor for cardiovascular disease than DBP. Among patients older than 65 years, SBP is a better predictor of cardiovascular events and mortality than diastolic pressure.
Untreated patients are at increased risk of developing complications such as atherosclerosis, cardiomegaly, congestive heart failure, retinopathy, stroke, renal insufficiency, and premature death.
BP should be treated to a target BP less than 140/90 to decrease cardiovascular complications.
Ambulatory 24 hours BP monitoring is a better predictor of mortality than clinic readings.

In patients with stage 1 hypertension and additional cardiac risk factors, achieving a sustained reduction of 12 mm Hg in SBP over 10 years will prevent 1 death for every 11 patients treated. In patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease or target organ damage treating nine patients for 10 years will prevent 1 death.
Consistent lowering of BP below 70 mm Hg diastolic in patients with coronary artery disease is associated with more bad outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, stroke).
Among patients with established hypertension, a single elevated BP reading can predict adverse events over the next 5 years.

Patients presenting in ambulatory clinics with blood pressure readings in the "hypertensive urgency" range, the majority have poorly controlled blood pressure at one month; adverse cardiovascular events at that same time, however, are low.

Seeing patients with controlled hypertension every 6 months, rather than every 3 months, results in similar BP measurements both in the office and at home, with no changes in patients satisfaction or adherence to therapy.
Home monitoring may be associated with increased visits to the emergency department.
Clinicians should provide to patients, verbally and in writing, their specific BP numbers and BP goals.
Books from the American Heart Association (1-800-638-0672; available at retail book stores): American Heart Association Low Salt Cookbook, American Heart Association Hypertension Primer (3rd Ed.).
See list of websites for information about physical activity (Shape Up America) and the DASH diet.

The Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program (SHEP) demonstrated that treating isolated systolic hypertension decreased the incidence of major cardiovascular events. This was confirmed by a Cochrane review of hypertension treatment in patients older than 60 years.
Furthermore, retrospective analysis of the SHEP data shows that among older patients, those with higher cardiovascular risk derived greater benefit of treatment.
In the Systolic Hypertension in Europe trial cardiovascular mortality was clearly decreased in the treatment of systolic hypertension.

The choice of antihypertensive can be based on factors such as cost, side effect profile, and patient preference, since all antihypertensives are equally effective in decreasing major cardiovascular events. BP treatment of older patients produces a similar reduction in events as does treatment of younger patients.
See chapter on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy.
The USPSTF recommends screening for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
A Cochrane review concluded that it is unclear that treating mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy is effective.

However, a subsequent study identified 2408 pregnant women with a gestational age of less than 23 weeks and a known or new diagnosis of mild chronic hypertension defined as at least 2 blood pressure measurements of 140 to 159 mm Hg systolic or 90 to 104 mm Hg diastolic. Patients with blood pressure of less than 140/90 were eligible if they had prior diagnosis of chronic hypertension. They randomized participants to a BP goal of 140/90 using nifedipine or labetalol or to a control group. The control group stopped taking antihypertensive medication unless blood pressure measurements were at least 160 mm Hg systolic and/or at least 105 diastolic. The primary outcome was a composite of preeclampsia with severe features occurring up to 2 weeks after delivery, medically indicated preterm birth at less than 35 weeks', placental abruption, and fetal/neonatal death and occurred less frequently in the active treatment group (30.2% vs 37.0%, p < .001; NNT = 15; 9 - 34). The most frequent components of the primary outcome were preeclampsia with severe features and medically indicated preterm birth, each of which was statistically significant. The safety outcomes of neonatal birthweight of less than the 10th percentile and severe neonatal complications were similar between groups.
There is also insufficient evidence to support the recommendation of one particular antihypertensive class for hypertension during pregnancy. Labetalol and nifedipine are through to be safest.

Immediate delivery for pregant women with nonsevere hypertensive disorder of pregnancy who are 34 to 37 weeks gestation is associated with increased neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, but expectant management may increase maternal risk.
Children older than 3 years who are seen in medical care settings should have their BP measured at least once during every health care episode.

A systematic review of 23 studies with 4210 children and adolescents identifed risk factors associated with the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with secondary hypertension. The overall prevalence of secondary hypertension in children was 9% in primary care settings and 44% in referral settings. Demographic findings most associated with secondary hypertension included a family history of secondary hypertension (LR+ 4.7), a history of prematurity (LR+ range 2.3 - 2.8), and age 6 years or younger (LR+ range 2.2 - 2.6). A family history of primary hypertension was associated with a lower likelihood of secondary hypertension (LR- 0.49). Clinical and laboratory findings most associated with secondary hypertension included a body weight at the 10% or lower level for age and sex (LR+ 4.5), microalbuminuria (LR+ 13), and a serum uric acid concentration of 5.5 mg/dL or lower with normal renal function (LR+ range 2.1 - 6.3). Clinical findings associated with a decreased likelihood of secondary hypertension included obesity (LR- 0.34) and the absence of hypertension-related symptoms (eg, headache, blurry vision, dizziness, chest pain, edema; LR- range 0.19 - 0.36).
NHLBI guidelines on cardiovascular health and risk reduction in children are available online. However, it was last updated in 2008.

Definition of hypertension in children and adolescents is a BP reading greater than the 95 percentile on three occasions using height-based tables. Children who fall in the 90 percentile to 95 percentile range on three occasions are prehypertensive, and need advice on lifestyle modification. Any adolescent with readings greater than 120/80 is prehypertensive.
A table summarizing normal vital signs in children from the University of Iowa is available online.
